hints: Focus on the very start of the reaction, when almost no product exists yet to act as a catalyst.
Think about what happens next as a little product forms and starts to catalyse its own formation.
Remember that near the end reactants run low, so even with catalyst present the rate must fall back toward zero.
walkthrough:
**Think about the start - no catalyst yet**

At time = 0, there is reactant but essentially no product. Since the catalyst is the product, there is no catalysis yet.

So initial rate $\approx 0$.

**Think about the middle - catalyst builds up**

As reaction proceeds slowly, product forms. That product catalyses the reaction, lowering $E_a$ and speeding it up.

So rate increases sharply, the reaction speeds itself up.

**Think about the end - reactants run out**

Later, even though catalyst is plentiful, the concentration of reactants becomes very low. Fewer successful collisions can happen.

So rate reaches a maximum then decreases toward zero, giving a rise-and-fall hump shape.

options.A: Incorrect. This shows rate starting fast and then staying high forever. In reality the rate must start near zero (no catalyst yet) and must fall at the end when reactants are used up, not level off at a high value.
options.B: Incorrect. This shows a slow start followed by a rise to a constant high rate. It correctly shows the autocatalytic speed-up but wrongly suggests the rate stays high. Reactant depletion must cause the rate to fall again.
options.C: Correct. Rate starts at zero, increases as catalytic product builds up, passes through a maximum, then decreases as reactant concentration falls. This rise-then-fall hump is characteristic of autocatalysis.
options.D: Incorrect. This is the normal rate-time curve for a non-catalysed reaction, fastest at the start when reactant concentration is highest, then steadily decreasing. It misses the key autocatalytic feature of a slow start that speeds up.
